summary: After a massive power outage hit Maplewood on September 5, 2023, the town began treating renewable energy as central to community resilience. The article describes the outage's cascading effects, local leaders' calls for energy self-determination, and measures like microgrids, battery storage, education programs, and smart grids. It also covers challenges such as cost and regulation, noting that solar costs have fallen sharply.
one_line: Maplewood's 2023 blackout prompted the town to adopt renewables, microgrids, storage, smart grids and energy education to strengthen community resilience.
key_facts: On September 5, 2023, a failure at a substation near Maplewood at 2:17 PM triggered a cascade of outages that left the town in darkness for days.
The outage was later linked to outdated infrastructure struggling under demand from a recent heatwave.
Over 15,000 residents, including businesses, hospitals, and schools, were affected by the Maplewood outage.
Martha Jensen, a local resident and small business owner, said the outage meant loss of communication, spoiled food, disrupted medical services, and a halt to daily operations.
Mayor Aidan Smith said the town must 'take charge of our energy destiny' so such vulnerability becomes a thing of the past.

Dr. Suresh Patel, an environmental scientist, said solar panels on school rooftops and the new wind farm are components of a decentralized grid that can isolate outages or keep running when the main grid fails.
On November 12, 2023, the Maplewood Town Council approved a measure to incorporate microgrids and battery storage systems into its emergency management plan.
Council member Liang Wu said microgrids provide energy independence that could be lifesaving in an emergency.
The Maplewood Renewable Energy Fair, led by high school teacher Elizabeth Gomez, aims to build energy literacy and demystify renewables.
Local contractor Jim Bates reported a 40% drop in solar installation costs over the past five years.
Cited obstacles to renewables include high initial costs, regulatory barriers, and scalability, offset partly by federal and state incentives.
Smart grid technologies and AI for predicting and managing energy flows can help prevent outages from escalating into blackouts.
Partnerships between local governments, private entities, and academic institutions have been instrumental in pioneering smart grid and AI projects.
